text: Every chapter so far has taught you one piece of Qiskit in isolation. The capstone asks you to do something different: wire those pieces together into one small, genuinely useful tool, and then be able to explain exactly what it's doing under the hood.

The tool has five jobs. Accept a simple circuit specification — a short list of gate tuples. Build the corresponding QuantumCircuit. Run it two ways: Statevector for the exact theoretical answer, and AerSimulator with a fixed shot count for an empirical distribution. Compare the two and automatically flag disagreements beyond a reasonable statistical threshold. And produce a written, gate-by-gate explanation of how the state evolved.

Notice what this is and isn't. You are not writing your own matrix-multiplication engine — Qiskit's Statevector and AerSimulator already do that correctly and efficiently. What you're building sits one layer above the engine, driving its existing simulation machinery in two different modes and adding a comparison and validation layer on top. That's a realistic shape for a lot of real engineering work.

Here's the trap this capstone is designed to avoid: building a tool, running it once, getting some numbers back, and assuming they're correct because the code didn't crash. The fix is a basic but genuinely important discipline — before trusting a tool on a case where you don't know the answer, run it on a case where you do, and confirm it reproduces that known answer.

The test case for the next three lessons is the same 3-qubit GHZ circuit from Chapter 2's lab: a Hadamard on qubit 0, followed by a chain of CX gates propagating entanglement outward. Its exact final state is already independently known — an equal superposition of |000> and |111>, with every other basis state at exactly zero amplitude — which is exactly what makes it a trustworthy case to validate the tool against before pointing it at anything new.
Next lesson turns requirements two and three into real code: a function that translates the spec into a circuit, and both the exact and shot-based simulation layers running against it.
